passage:
Counsellor's note, Thursday. Observed at the athletics ground, 4 p.m.
Coach asked Keerthana (15, squad captain) to run a punishment set for Sahil, who had missed Monday's practice. First it was 'two laps, just to remind him.' Keerthana blew the whistle and held the stopwatch. After the second lap Sahil was bent over, and she looked at Coach. Coach said calmly, 'Continue. It's for his own good.' Keerthana's hands were shaking on the stopwatch. She said 'one more' four more times, each time quieter, glancing back at Coach instead of at Sahil.
At that point I walked over, stopped the set and sat Sahil in the shade with water. Keerthana burst into tears: 'I didn't know how to stop once I'd started.' I spoke with her afterwards and raised the punishment laps with the head of sports the same afternoon.

qa.q: How many laps was the punishment set at first?
qa.a: At first it was 'two laps, just to remind him.'

qa.q: What does Keerthana glancing back at Coach instead of at Sahil suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Keerthana was full of doubt and leaning on Coach's calm to carry the responsibility, rather than facing Sahil's distress.

qa.q: Where was the easiest point for Keerthana to stop, and why?
qa.a: After the second lap, when Sahil was bent over; as Keerthana said, it got harder to stop once each 'one more' had piled up.

qa.q: How might Sahil have experienced his own captain calling 'one more'?
qa.a: Sahil might feel let down by his captain, while also noticing her voice growing quieter, as if she didn't want to do it.

grounding: A counsellor's note shows a teenage captain continuing a coach's calm punishment set step by step while visibly distressed.

passage:
Sunday night. I feel sick. Lakshmi-di is directing the annual play and I'm her assistant, so on Wednesday when she said, 'Move Rupa to the back row, she's too short for the front,' I did it. Easy. Thursday: 'Give Rupa's two lines to Anu.' I did that too, even though Rupa had practised them in the corridor all week. Today di said, calm as anything, 'Just tell her she's out. You've done the hard part already.' And somehow that was true: saying no now felt like saying the last four days were wrong. So I told Rupa. My voice shook the whole time and afterwards I went to the washroom and cried. Why was stopping harder than carrying on?
— Bidisha

qa.q: What did Lakshmi-di ask on Thursday?
qa.a: 'Give Rupa's two lines to Anu.'

qa.q: Why did saying no feel so hard for Bidisha by Sunday?
qa.a: Bidisha felt trapped: refusing now would mean the last four days were wrong, so carrying on seemed easier than stopping.

qa.q: Which day would have been the best point for Bidisha to push back, and how?
qa.a: Wednesday, at the first small step: Bidisha could have calmly asked why height mattered and suggested keeping Rupa in the front row.

qa.q: How might Rupa see these four days?
qa.a: Rupa, who practised her lines in the corridor all week, would likely feel pushed out bit by bit and hurt that it came through Bidisha 😢

grounding: A teenager's diary shows a senior's calm, step-by-step instructions leading them to cut a junior from a play while distressed.

passage: The scout camp was held in the school ground of a kasba outside Satara. Ganga, fifteen, was patrol leader, and the senior troop leader, Farhan, was a college boy everyone admired. When little Sonu came to assembly without his scarf, Farhan said calmly, "Ganga, make him stand in the sun. Just five minutes." Ganga did. Five minutes later: "Now arms out. Just continue." She hesitated. Sonu's lips were dry. "It's discipline. Continue," Farhan said, without raising his voice. Ganga's throat was tight, and her voice shook as she said, "Arms up, Sonu." Stopping now felt like saying the first five minutes were wrong. Then the scout teacher, Mrs Pillai, crossed the ground, stopped it at once, sat Sonu in the shade with water, and spoke to Farhan and Ganga separately before lunch.

qa.q: What did Sonu forget to bring to assembly?
qa.a: He came without his scarf.

qa.q: What was Ganga feeling as she kept giving the orders?
qa.a: She felt tense and doubtful, her throat tight and her voice shaking, yet stopping felt harder because it would mean the first step had been wrong.

qa.q: At what point could Ganga have stopped, and how?
qa.a: At the first order she could have said calmly that making Sonu stand in the sun was not right, before each small step made stopping harder.

qa.q: How did it feel for Sonu to be punished through Ganga?
qa.a: Sonu was left thirsty and exposed in the sun, made to obey an older scout, with no one stepping in until the teacher came.

passage: The school newspaper office in Accra smelled of printer ink. Yara, sixteen, had just joined as a junior editor, and Nkechi, the senior editor, was someone she wanted to impress. "Review Kwesi's poem for Friday's issue," Nkechi said calmly. "Be honest. Start with the rhymes." Yara wrote that the rhymes were weak. Nkechi read over her shoulder. "Good. Now add a line about how it sounds like a birthday card." Yara typed it. Her stomach clenched. "And say readers deserve better. Just continue, you're doing fine." Yara's fingers hovered. Kwesi was in Form 2 and had shown her the poem in the corridor, shyly. But she had already written two lines; deleting them now felt like admitting she'd been wrong from the start. She typed the third sentence with her face burning, and felt, strangely, like she was watching someone else do it.

qa.q: What did Nkechi tell Yara to start with in the review?
qa.a: Nkechi told Yara to start with the rhymes.

qa.q: What was Yara feeling when her fingers hovered over the keyboard?
qa.a: She was torn and distressed, knowing Kwesi had shyly shown her the poem, but deleting the first lines felt like admitting she had been wrong.

qa.q: What could Yara still do before Friday's issue goes out?
qa.a: She could tell Nkechi she is not comfortable publishing a mocking review and rewrite it as fair, kind feedback, since the review is not printed yet.

qa.q: How might Kwesi feel if the review is published as it is?
qa.a: Kwesi would probably feel humiliated in front of the school, especially after trusting Yara enough to show the poem in the corridor.

grounding: A teenager guided calmly by a senior writes a harsher and harsher review of a junior's poem, distressed but finding it harder to stop than to continue.

passage:

Wednesday: Yamini shouted "Move it!" at Anirban. It felt wrong. Coach nodded. By the end of practice she was shouting "Useless!" Each time was a little worse, and each time Coach said, "Good. Continue." Her throat was tight and her hands shook. Stopping now felt harder than going on.
Friday: Anirban didn't come to practice. Yamini sat on the bench, knees pulled up, feeling sick. After practice she went to the school counsellor and told her everything. The counsellor listened, said she'd speak to the sports head that day, and asked Yamini to walk with her to find Anirban.

qa.a: He was slow because he'd just recovered from a fracture.

qa.q: What was Yamini feeling while she kept shouting?
qa.a: Yamini felt tense and distressed, her throat tight and hands shaking, yet stopping felt harder than going on.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what finally helped?
qa.a: Small steps and Coach's calm "Continue" pulled Yamini further; going to the counsellor, who acted that day, broke the pattern.

qa.q: How might Anirban have felt by Friday?
qa.a: Anirban probably felt humiliated and unsafe, which may be why he stopped coming to practice.

passage: Meenal, you asked me why I won't let you join that hockey team's "tradition." Let me tell you. I'm Charu mausi. At sixteen I was on the district team in Jalandhar. The captain, a calm, older girl everyone admired, told me before a match: "Hide Preeti's stick. Just for fun. It's a welcome thing." Preeti was a new girl. I felt a twist in my stomach, but the captain smiled and said, "Just do it." So I hid it. Then she said, "Now tell Preeti the coach dropped her." My mouth went dry. I did that too. Preeti sat outside the ground and cried. The captain said, "Good, you're one of us now." I kept going, one step after another, feeling worse at each. At night I told my mother, and she went to the coach the very next morning. I still wish I'd stopped at the stick.

qa.q: What did the captain tell Charu to hide?
qa.a: The captain told her to hide Preeti's stick.

qa.q: What was Charu feeling as she followed the captain's orders?
qa.a: Charu felt a twist of dread and growing guilt, but the captain's calm manner made stopping feel harder than going on.

qa.q: Where in the story could Charu most easily have stopped, and why?
qa.a: At the very first step, hiding the stick, because each later step felt harder to refuse once she had begun.

qa.q: How might Preeti have felt sitting outside the ground?
qa.a: Preeti likely felt rejected and humiliated, believing she'd been dropped from the team.

passage: The NCC camp ground in Nagpur was baking at forty degrees. Senior cadet Baljeet told Kavitha, sixteen, "Make the juniors hold the plank. Two minutes. Discipline." Kavitha felt uneasy but nodded; it was only two minutes. When the time was up, Baljeet said calmly, "Another two." Some juniors were shaking. Kavitha's heart was racing. "Continue," Baljeet said, without raising his voice. She counted again, hating her own voice. One small boy's arms buckled and he lay face-down, gasping. Kavitha's legs moved before she thought. She knelt, helped him sit up in the shade, and handed him her water bottle. "Enough," she said to Baljeet, shaking. Then she ran to the officer's tent and reported it. The officer came out at once, ended the drill, and had the boy checked by the camp medic.

qa.a: The camp ground was baking at forty degrees.

It was the kabaddi team's evening practice in a Nagpur school ground. Tushar, the senior captain, pointed at the new junior who had come late. "Pankaj, make him do ten push-ups."
Ten was fine. Pankaj counted.
"Now twenty. Discipline matters." Tushar's voice was calm, almost bored.
The junior's arms were shaking. Pankaj's throat went tight. Should he say something? But he had already done ten. Stopping now would look like saying Tushar was wrong.
"Keep going," Tushar said. "Just continue."
Pankaj kept counting. His voice cracked on fourteen. The junior's face was red and wet.
At seventeen, the PE teacher came across the ground. "Stop. Now." She knelt by the junior. Pankaj sat down on the grass, his hands trembling.

qa.q: How many push-ups did Tushar first ask for?
qa.a: He first asked for ten push-ups.

qa.q: What was Pankaj feeling as his voice cracked on fourteen?
qa.a: He felt tense and distressed, doubting it was right, but stopping felt harder than going on because he had already started.

qa.q: What could Pankaj have done at the first doubt?
qa.a: He could have stopped counting and said the junior had done enough, or gone to find the PE teacher himself.

qa.q: How might the junior have felt doing push-ups while two seniors watched?
qa.a: The junior would have felt humiliated and exhausted, with no way to refuse two seniors.

passage:
I was fifteen when Coach Jeevan picked me for the district football final. I'm Darshan. Before the match he took me aside. "Their number 9 is their best. Just a small bump early. Make him nervous."
A bump. That seemed okay. In the first ten minutes I bumped him.
At half-time Coach said, "Good. Now a harder one. Leave a mark. Just continue what you started."
I felt sick. I remember my knees shaking in the tunnel. But I'd already done the first one. Stopping felt like admitting the first was wrong too.
In the second half I tackled number 9 from behind. He went down holding his ankle.
We won. I've never felt worse after a win.

qa.a: He asked for just a small bump early.

qa.q: What was Darshan feeling in the tunnel at half-time?
qa.a: Darshan felt sick and afraid, knowing a harder tackle was wrong but feeling trapped by having already done the first.

qa.q: What could Darshan have done at the first doubt?
qa.a: Darshan could have refused the first bump, when saying no was easiest, or told the coach the plan felt unfair.

qa.q: How might number 9 have felt going down holding his ankle?
qa.a: He would have felt pain and shock, and maybe anger at being targeted on purpose.

Assistant coach's note, athletics camp, day 3.
The head coach told Sharmila, the team captain, to 'toughen up' Kiran, a new runner who had missed a morning session. It started small: one extra lap. Then another. The coach kept saying, calmly, 'Continue. It's for his own good.' By the sixth lap in the midday heat, Kiran was stumbling and asking to stop. Sharmila was biting her lip, glancing at the coach, clearly upset, but she kept counting laps aloud. When I stepped in and stopped it, she burst into tears. 'I wanted to stop after two. But he was so calm, and I'd already done two.' I sat Kiran in the shade with water and called the camp doctor. I reported the instruction to the camp director immediately, and spoke with Sharmila, who asked to talk to Kiran herself tonight.

passage:
Thursday night.
I can't stop thinking about rehearsal. Rhea Didi, the drama club head, told me to 'coach' Asif from Class 8 because he stammers on his lines. First she said, make him repeat the line. Fine. Then, make him say it louder. Then, in front of everyone, make him say it until he gets it right. Asif's face went red, then white. I kept looking at Rhea Didi, and she just nodded and said, calmly, 'Continue, he needs this.' And I did. Four more times. My hands were shaking. I felt like two people: one saying 'again', one screaming stop. It felt harder to stop than to go on, because I'd already started. After, Asif ran out. I told Ms Fernandes before I left school, and she found Asif and called his parents. Tomorrow I'm apologising.
Keerthana

qa.q: What did Rhea Didi say when Asif went red?
qa.a: 'Continue, he needs this.'

qa.q: What was Keerthana feeling while making Asif repeat the line?
qa.a: Keerthana felt torn and distressed, hands shaking, one part saying 'again' and another screaming to stop.

qa.q: What made it hard to stop, and what could help next time?
qa.a: The calm authority and having already started; next time Keerthana could stop at the first doubt, say no, or go straight to a teacher.

qa.q: How was the rehearsal for Asif?
qa.a: Asif felt humiliated and frightened, going red then white before running out.
